doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Catatonic Five and the earlier Fallacious Five
summary: The Fallacious Five came before; they stood on earlier players' shoulders; reflections on age gaps.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: What’s the connection between the Catatonic Five and the Fallacious Five? Was that a little bit before?

That was before. And I think Emerson and Donny perhaps were the — that was, you know Paul Parker was here when I was a student. He was a professor but he played some but not a great deal. But that was a little before. And you stand on the shoulders of giants. That’s what got it all started. And then we just came at the right time.

Isn’t it interesting, at least I feel in those times, when you’re 18 and someone’s 21 back in those times, and they have more experience, they just seem so much older and wiser and everything. Then you get older and three years is almost nothing.
It’s a lifetime, and particularly you’re coming from high school to college, and then an upper classman, wow.
